title: Conventional-oil recovery at gas-field recovery factors

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a practical way to recover roughly 80 percent or more of the original oil in place from heterogeneous conventional reservoirs, while keeping energy use, chemical costs and operating logistics comparable to waterflooding. It concerns reservoirs in which oil already flows. Achieving the target would require both releasing oil retained within the pore network and bringing injected fluids into contact with oil that conventional floods bypass.

The concept specifies an outcome rather than a particular chemical or injection process. A successful system might combine changes to fluid properties, mobility control and reservoir management. Its defining capability would be sustained, economical recovery across substantial reservoir volumes. The gas-field comparison names the intended recovery ambition; the supplied evidence does not establish 80 percent as a universal gas-field benchmark or show that conventional oil can generally attain it.

significance.text: If widely transferable, the proposed capability would substantially increase the recoverable yield of already discovered conventional accumulations. The gain would depend on each field’s baseline recovery: fields with substantial trapped or bypassed oil would have more room for improvement. Comparable costs and logistics would be central to the significance, because technically recoverable oil does not automatically become commercially recoverable oil.

Higher ultimate recovery could extend productive field life and, where deployment succeeds, increase cumulative output from existing developments. It would not establish a proportional increase in production rate or immediately multiply economic supply. Those outcomes would also depend on injection and production capacity, remaining field life, deployment time and operating constraints. The supplied material does not support a single supply multiplier.

The analogy with gas recovery has a physical limit. Oil recovery must contend with pore-scale retention and incomplete reservoir contact, and excellent displacement within contacted rock can coexist with poor overall recovery. The historical review cited in the research provides the framework for these distinctions, although its text was not available to the supplied reviewer. The concept therefore requires field-scale performance rather than a direct transfer of a gas recovery percentage to oil.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability is coordinated control of displacement efficiency and reservoir sweep under practical field conditions. Displacement efficiency describes how much oil an injected fluid removes from the rock it contacts; sweep describes how much of the oil-bearing reservoir it reaches. These are two central barriers, rather than an exhaustive statement of every recovery limit, and their relative importance varies by reservoir. Improving one can leave the other as the dominant constraint.

At the pore scale, the supplied research attributes to Muggeridge and colleagues a typical waterflood capillary number of approximately 2.5×10^−7, with capillary trapping dominant below roughly 10^−5. It also reports an estimate that oil–water interfacial tension must fall below approximately 0.1 mN/m to minimize trapping. These quantities illustrate the proposed gap between ordinary flooding and effective mobilization; they should not be treated as universal thresholds. The same account describes snap-off in water-wet pores, in which oil becomes disconnected into trapped bodies. The reviewer could not inspect the source text to verify these numerical values, their conditions or the mechanism’s stated scope.

At reservoir scale, preferential flow through more permeable pathways can leave substantial oil-bearing rock unswept. The research describes bypassed volumes at scales that available seismic surveying cannot resolve. It also reports residual oil saturation near 2 percent in reservoir cores from gas-swept zones. Even if confirmed, that local measurement would establish efficient displacement only within contacted rock. Mobile, buoyant gas can still channel or override oil elsewhere, preventing comparably high field recovery. These source-attributed details remain unverified against retained document text.

The engineering challenge is to preserve complementary improvements under actual reservoir conditions. The supplied research discusses low-salinity water, polymers and surfactants as approaches that affect different parts of the recovery problem, with temperature, salinity and rock chemistry restricting which formulations remain useful. A broadly useful system would need to mobilize oil, maintain effective reservoir contact and remain operable at acceptable cost across the conditions it claims to serve. The evidence supplied does not establish that any single formulation can meet that combination.

current_state.text: The supplied evidence base consists of research attributed to the 2014 review “Recovery rates, enhanced oil recovery and technological limits.” The source index contains no captured document or extracted text, so the reviewer could not independently verify its passages, numerical examples or locators. The examples below are therefore historical results reported by the supplied research. The record contains no later evidence establishing the frontier as of November 1, 2026; this limitation leaves subsequent progress unknown and does not show that the reported results are false.

For Magnus, the research reports that approximately 40 percent of oil initially in place had been recovered when seawater breakthrough occurred, and that surfactant-polymer flooding was rejected because the reservoir temperature was 115 °C. These describe a particular field history and a reported process-selection constraint. They do not establish Magnus’s ultimate recovery, a universal temperature limit for chemical flooding or the maximum recovery attainable elsewhere. The underlying event dates and source passages were not available for verification.

For Clair Ridge, the research attributes reductions in residual oil saturation of approximately 5.6 to 7.6 percentage points to low-salinity coreflood experiments. These are laboratory changes in saturation within tested rock. They are not equivalent to a 5.6-to-7.6-percentage-point increase in field recovery of original oil in place, because field performance also depends on reservoir contact and other operating conditions. The supplied record does not verify the experiments’ dates, conditions or detailed saturation definitions.

The earlier assertion that the best published field combinations achieve about 50–70 percent recovery is not established by the supplied evidence. The cited historical examples cannot support a present-day ranking or upper band. Likewise, this record does not establish whether the full proposed combination—roughly 80 percent or greater field recovery, heterogeneous-reservoir performance and waterflood-comparable practical costs—has subsequently been demonstrated. Its achievement and its continued absence both remain unproven here.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: achieve approximately 80 percent or greater cumulative recovery of original oil in place in at least one heterogeneous conventional sandstone reservoir and one heterogeneous conventional carbonate reservoir. Each demonstration should involve a multi-year flood at well spacing representative of ordinary development for that reservoir class. These are proposed acceptance criteria for this concept, not established industry standards. Two successful demonstrations would establish meaningful breadth across the tested conditions, while leaving wider applicability to be demonstrated.
completion_criteria.label: Achieve approximately 80% cumulative recovery in heterogeneous sandstone and carbonate

completion_criteria.text: Recovery should be supported by an explicit estimate of original oil in place, cumulative production accounting and uncertainty bounds. The assessment should distinguish oil already produced before the intervention, incremental recovery attributable to the new system and recovery still projected. A forecast of eventual 80 percent recovery would be useful supporting evidence but would not satisfy a criterion framed as achieved cumulative recovery. Changes in estimated oil in place should be disclosed so that a revised denominator cannot masquerade as improved physical recovery.
completion_criteria.label: Report achieved recovery accounting with oil-in-place estimates and uncertainty bounds

completion_criteria.text: The practical comparison should define a credible waterflood alternative for each reservoir and disclose the accounting boundary. It should report energy consumption and chemical expenditure per recovered barrel, together with injection requirements, fluid handling and operating logistics. The proposal’s phrase “in the waterflood range” needs an agreed numerical interpretation before testing. Recovery purchased through substantially greater drilling, energy use or chemical consumption would need to be assessed against the original practical ambition.
completion_criteria.label: Quantify full resource costs against numerically defined waterflood alternatives

completion_criteria.text: Corefloods and single-pattern pilots would provide intermediate evidence but would not satisfy the proposed field-scale criterion. Convincing validation would include reproducible measurements, independently reviewable recovery estimates and sufficient operating detail to distinguish local displacement improvements from sustained reservoir sweep. Additional deployments should establish transferability and identify boundaries in temperature, salinity, permeability structure and rock chemistry. Finite demonstrations establish the range actually tested; they cannot prove universal applicability. Shale-oil matrix recovery, tight-rock access and immobile bitumen remain outside this proposal.
completion_criteria.label: Validate sustained reservoir sweep with reproducible, independently reviewable field-scale evidence

related_concepts.text: Based on the supplied titles, PET-01, “Blind prediction of multiphase reservoir flow,” concerns predicting reservoir behavior, while PET-02 concerns achieving a physical recovery outcome. Better predictions could help design and assess recovery processes, but prediction accuracy alone would not mobilize or sweep oil. PET-08, “Permeability and saturation measured through the reservoir volume,” could help identify bypassed oil and evaluate reservoir contact. Measurement and prediction are plausible enablers; neither is equivalent to high recovery. These relationships are inferred from the roster because the full entries were not supplied.

PET-05, “Shale-oil recovery from the matrix,” and PET-09, “Bitumen that flows at native reservoir temperature,” address resource classes explicitly excluded from PET-02. The former concerns recovery from shale matrix; the latter concerns making bitumen flow under native conditions. PET-11, “In-reservoir conversion of bitumen to pipeline-specification crude,” adds an in-reservoir conversion and product-quality objective. Their titles indicate distinct access, mobility or conversion goals, so a conventional-oil recovery success would not establish their completion. Detailed mechanistic overlap cannot be assessed without their full records.

PET-07, “Deep well construction without a steep depth penalty,” could affect the cost of reaching or developing some reservoirs. PET-10, “A pressure plan with a prospectively tested earthquake bound,” concerns a constraint that could matter to injection-based deployment. Neither title specifies the displacement and sweep capability required here. Their possible contribution is enabling access or operating conditions, with the actual relationship dependent on the methods used.

The remaining roster entries pursue different production objectives: PET-03 concerns commercial gas production from methane hydrate; PET-04 concerns industrial in-situ conversion of oil-shale kerogen; and PET-06 concerns hydrogen production from petroleum reservoirs while leaving other products underground. They share a broad subsurface-resource setting with PET-02, but their supplied titles do not establish a shared completion criterion or a direct technical dependency.

change_log.change: Preserved PET-02’s identity, title and ambitious conventional-oil recovery objective while making its hypothetical status explicit.
change_log.reason: The review identifies a coherent proposed capability; gaps in supporting evidence do not invalidate the concept.

change_log.change: Integrated pore-scale trapping, reservoir sweep, gas mobility and chemical compatibility into distinct explanations of the missing capability.
change_log.reason: The research supplies useful mechanisms, while the review requires qualification of their verification and reservoir-dependent importance.

change_log.change: Retained the capillary-number, interfacial-tension and gas-swept residual-saturation figures as source-attributed, unverified details rather than universal limits.
change_log.reason: No source artifact was available for inspection, but lack of inspection does not establish that the figures are incorrect.

change_log.change: Replaced the claim that exactly two mechanisms set the ceiling with displacement and sweep as two central, reservoir-dependent barriers.
change_log.reason: The review cautions that their importance varies and that the original wording was overly exhaustive.

change_log.change: Removed the asserted current 50–70 percent frontier and avoided claiming that the proposed breakthrough remains absent today.
change_log.reason: A 2014 source and no later evidence cannot establish a current ranking or the absence of subsequent achievement.

change_log.change: Preserved the Magnus and Clair Ridge examples as historical reports and separated laboratory saturation changes from field recovery.
change_log.reason: The examples retain explanatory value, but their passages were not verified and their measurement scales differ.

change_log.change: Reframed the impact as a conditional increase in recoverable yield, without an unspecified supply multiplier or an assumed production-rate increase.
change_log.reason: Commercial supply depends on baseline recovery, transferability, deployment and operating constraints.

change_log.change: Expanded the proposed completion criteria to cover uncertainty, achieved versus projected recovery, comparator accounting, reproducibility and transferability.
change_log.reason: The original proposal needed operational definitions to make a field demonstration convincing and reviewable.

change_log.change: Used the supplied roster to explain related concepts while labeling relationships as title-based inferences.
change_log.reason: The roster permits limited comparison, although the full related entries were unavailable to the reviewer.

unresolved_issues: The sole indexed source has no captured artifact or extracted text. Its reported mechanisms, numerical thresholds, historical examples and contextual qualifications remain unverified.
No supplied evidence establishes the recovery frontier as of November 1, 2026 or whether the full proposed capability has subsequently been demonstrated.
The approximately 80 percent gas-field comparison remains an ambition in this record; its representativeness across gas fields is unestablished.
The reported 5.6-to-7.6-percentage-point Clair Ridge saturation reduction needs confirmation against the original measurement definitions and experimental conditions.
The demonstration protocol still needs numerical definitions for waterflood-comparable costs and energy, representative well spacing, accounting boundaries and acceptable recovery uncertainty.
Full records for the related PET concepts are unavailable, so their technical dependencies and overlaps remain provisional.

brief.title: Affordable recovery of most oil from existing fields
possible: Oil producers could recover roughly 80% of the oil originally held in existing fields where oil already flows. The system would free oil trapped in tiny rock spaces and reach oil that injected water bypasses, while keeping energy use, chemical costs and operations comparable to ordinary water injection.
why: Already discovered fields could yield substantially more oil and stay productive longer. Operators would gain more usable output from existing developments, with the largest gains where much oil remains trapped or bypassed.

sources.showed: This review examines oil recovery methods and the physical limits imposed by oil trapped within rock and by injected fluids failing to reach it.
sources.cited_for: It explains why freeing trapped oil and reaching bypassed oil are separate challenges.
sources.not_established: It does not establish economical recovery of most original oil across whole fields.

sources.showed: A West Salym field pilot used injected chemicals to recover extra oil. Returning chemicals also caused pump failures through mineral deposits and persistent oil-water mixtures. The conference report was not peer reviewed.
sources.quote: The ASP injection resulted in the mobilization of a significant volume of oil in the confined 5-spot pattern.
sources.cited_for: The pilot demonstrates extra oil recovery alongside practical operating problems.
sources.not_established: A confined pilot does not establish the target recovery across a whole field or costs comparable to ordinary water injection.

sources.showed: Tests on rock samples from a Kazakhstani sandstone field recovered much of the oil left after water injection. The team recommended a simpler chemical blend for pilot testing because adding alkali brought little extra recovery.
sources.quote:
producing more than 90% of the remaining oil after 
waterflooding.
sources.cited_for: Chemical blends can remove much of the oil remaining in contacted rock.
sources.not_established: Recovery from laboratory rock samples does not establish how much oil injected chemicals would reach across a field.

sources.who: Douglas Arnell, Malcolm Pitts and Jie Qi
sources.showed: Laboratory tests using Poison Spider field rock and fluids reached average total recovery of 64.6% in tests with outward flow. The team also prepared a field implementation outline.
sources.quote: Chemical solutions injected into and flowed through Poison Spider rock.
sources.cited_for: The work demonstrates chemical compatibility and additional recovery in laboratory rock tests.
sources.not_established: Laboratory performance and an implementation outline do not establish sustained field recovery or actual operating costs.

sources.who: Shahla Kaabi Mofrad and Amir Hossein Saeedi Dehaghani
sources.showed: Water with adjusted salt content and chemicals that help oil and water mix recovered 58% of the oil in a glass model patterned after carbonate rock.
sources.cited_for: Combining adjusted water chemistry with added chemicals improved recovery in a laboratory model.
sources.not_established: A glass model does not establish recovery, chemical performance or costs in a working carbonate field.

shown: The strongest field result described is Volokitin and colleagues’ West Salym pilot. It estimated additional recovery above 16% of the oil originally in the pilot area, but also encountered serious operating problems.
Laboratory studies show that chemicals can free oil left behind by water injection. The central gap is carrying that performance through a large, uneven reservoir while keeping operations affordable.
missing: Sustained recovery at the target level across substantial reservoir volumes, including both trapped and bypassed oil.
Measured energy use, chemical expenditure and operating demands comparable to a clearly defined water-injection alternative.
Independent field validation that separates achieved recovery from forecasts and demonstrates performance across different reservoir conditions.

milestones.label: Target recovery in sandstone and carbonate fields
milestones.explanation: Trials lasting several years would have to recover about 80% of original oil in sandstone and carbonate reservoirs with uneven flow paths, using normal well spacing. This would test the goal across different rocks.

milestones.label: Achieved recovery with clear uncertainty
milestones.explanation: Recovery accounting would have to estimate original oil and uncertainty, separating earlier production, added recovery and forecasts. This would establish a physical gain rather than a changed estimate.

milestones.label: Full costs comparable to ordinary water injection
milestones.explanation: Field results would have to compare energy, chemicals, drilling, injection and fluid handling against a numerically defined water-injection alternative. This would establish whether higher recovery remains practical.

milestones.label: Sustained reservoir contact confirmed across field deployments
milestones.explanation: Reproducible field measurements open to independent review would have to show sustained contact with oil-bearing rock, with further deployments testing transferability. This would distinguish local success from broad reservoir coverage.

uncertain: How comparable costs and energy use, representative well spacing and acceptable recovery uncertainty should be defined remains unsettled.
How far successful methods would transfer across temperature, salt content, rock chemistry and uneven flow paths remains open.
